big_idea: This Harvard Business Review anthology argues that strategy is not a single technique but a discipline with several distinct, sometimes competing schools -- positioning (Porter), value innovation (Kim/Mauborgne), business-model design (Johnson/Christensen), and execution discipline -- and compiles the articles considered most foundational to each.

tool.label: Porter's Five Forces / Activity-Fit Framework (from the featured article 'What Is Strategy?')
tool.text: The anchor article argues operational effectiveness is not strategy because competitors can copy it; real strategy means choosing a distinct position and making explicit trade-offs -- deliberately choosing not to do certain things. Porter shows this with Southwest Airlines, which forgoes meals and seat assignments to sustain a uniquely low-cost position. The framework's deeper claim is about fit: competitive advantage comes from activities reinforcing one another, which is why rivals struggle to imitate a whole system even when they can copy individual pieces.
tool.note: Because this is a curated anthology spanning multiple authors and decades, the tools inside genuinely conflict with each other in places -- Porter's trade-off-driven positioning sits uneasily next to Kim/Mauborgne's value-innovation logic.

ideas.title: Strategy vs. operational effectiveness
ideas.text: Porter's opening distinction -- that doing existing activities better is not the same as choosing a different, defensible position -- sets the frame for the collection.

ideas.title: Business model reinvention
ideas.text: Johnson, Christensen, and Kagermann's article breaks a business model into four interlocking parts as a diagnostic for whether a new opportunity needs a genuinely new model.

ideas.title: Blue ocean value curves
ideas.text: The Kim/Mauborgne article condenses their book's strategy-canvas logic into a standalone piece.

ideas.title: Building a durable vision
ideas.text: Collins and Porras separate a company's timeless core ideology from its changeable strategies and practices.

ideas.title: The balanced scorecard as a management system
ideas.text: Kaplan and Norton's article extends their scorecard into a full system for translating strategy into operational targets.

ideas.title: Who has the D (decision rights)
ideas.text: Rogers and Blenko argue execution fails most often from unclear decision rights, offering the RAPID framework for assigning them.

try_it: Read the Porter and Kim/Mauborgne articles back to back and write down where their advice would actually conflict for your specific business.
Apply the four-part business model framework to a new initiative your team is considering.
Identify one recurring decision where it's genuinely unclear who has final authority, and propose a RAPID-style assignment for it.
Separate your team's core purpose from its current tactics using the Collins/Porras lens, and check whether recent changes have blurred the two.
best_for: MBA students, consultants, or managers who want a single-volume survey of the most-cited strategy frameworks.
Executives building an internal strategy curriculum who need canonical, HBR-vetted source material to cite.
less_useful: Readers who want one coherent, end-to-end methodology -- the anthology format means switching frameworks and voices every 20-30 pages.
Anyone who has already read the original full-length books several of these articles are condensed from.

related.why: Blue Ocean Strategy is the full-length source for one of this anthology's featured articles.
Good Strategy/Bad Strategy complements Porter's positioning logic with a sharper diagnostic method.
